newsitem.title: FRANCE: French museums to exhibit art taken by Nazis.
newsitem.headline: French museums to exhibit art taken by Nazis.

text.p: Some 900 works of art the Nazis took from France during World War Two will go on display next month in four Paris museums in the hope their owners will claim them, museum officials said on Wednesday.

The works, including paintings by Picasso and Matisse, were returned from Germany after the war. Unclaimed, they were temporarily entrusted to state-run museums, who were required by law to try to find their rightful owners.

It is widely believed some of the pieces were seized from Jews who were deported to concentration camps or who sold them under duress at rock-bottom prices, while others were sold to Nazi officers by art dealers.
The exhibits will open on April 8 at the Musee d'Orsay and the following day at the Louvre, the Pompidou Centre and the Musee National de la Ceramique. They are expected to run about two weeks.
The works also include paintings by Cezanne, Utrillo, Raoul Dufy, Fernand Leger and Gustave Courbet.
"Some of the works have been exhibited (in museums), but others that are less important have been in storage," said Benedicte Moreau of the Direction des Musees de France, the state museum network.
She said that museums in the provinces in possession of such works "had been invited to hold their own exhibits".
The display follows a government decision to launch an inquiry into Jewish property -- artwork, apartments, jewels, bank accounts -- seized during Germany's occupation of France.

In January, the Cour des Comptes state auditing body accused national museum officials of having failed in their legal duty to try and return some 1,995 works that have been in their collections since being returned to France after the war. The works are known as MNR (national museum-recovery).

The MNR are what is left of a total of some 61,000 works repatriated to France, 45,000 of which were recovered by their owners in the years immediately following the war. Others of little value were sold at auctions.
"It's a start, but they have to go further," said journalist Hector Feliciano, whose book "The Lost Museum" revived the issue of the MNR.

"It proves that under public pressure, the museums have taken a more reasonable position. After remaining silent and oblivious for years, they have admitted their errors and are attempting to rectify them," he said. "But it's not enough to exhibit the art, the owners' heirs must be actively sought."

Feliciano said that a statue by Auguste Rodin, "Le Baiser" (The Kiss), which is in the garden of the prime minister's Matignon headquarters, and a bust of king Louis XV's mistress Madame Pompadour at the Elysee presidential palace are MNR.
